Course Description 
This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of key areas of Canadian law, 
emphasizing both theoretical knowledge and practical application. Students will explore property 
law, dispute resolution, negligence, controversial legal issues, landmark court decisions, and 
criminal law. Through case studies, simulations, and research projects, students will develop 
critical thinking, problem-solving, and legal analysis skills while understanding the impact of 
law on individuals and society. This course prepares students for informed citizenship, post-
secondary studies in law, and careers in justice-related fields. 
 
Course Objectives 
• Differentiate between various areas of Canadian law and their applications. 
• Analyze legal disputes and propose appropriate resolution strategies. 
• Examine negligence and legal responsibilities within personal and societal contexts. 
• Evaluate controversial legal issues and appreciate multiple perspectives. 
• Investigate landmark court decisions and their influence on Canadian law and society. 
• Understand the structure and principles of the Canadian criminal justice system. 
• Apply critical thinking and problem-solving skills to legal scenarios. 
• Conduct research, present findings, and articulate legal arguments in multiple formats.

COURSE LGS3010: PROPERTY LAW 
 
Description: Students identify laws relating to real, personal and intellectual properties and 
investigate the processes of buying and selling real property and the legal implications associated 
with Internet transactions. 
 
Property refers to legally recognized rights to possess, use, enjoy, and dispose of something. In 
law, property is not the object itself, but the bundle of rights attached to it. 
 
Real, Personal, and Intellectual Property. In Canadian law, property refers to legally 
recognized rights to own, use, control, and transfer something. Property is commonly classified 
into real property, personal property, and intellectual property. 
 
Real Property (Real Estate): Includes land and anything permanently attached to the land. 
Ownership of real property is registered and governed by provincial legislation. 
• Characteristics: Immovable, Fixed to the land, Often high in value, Ownership is 
recorded on land title 
• Examples: Land and lots, Houses and apartment buildings, Farms and commercial 
buildings, Fixtures such as built-in cabinets or plumbing, Mineral rights (unless separated 
from the surface title) 
• Relevant Alberta Legislation: Law of Property Act, Land Titles Act 
 
Personal Property (Chattels): Refers to movable items that are not permanently attached to 
land. These items can be bought, sold, leased, or used as security for loans. 
• Characteristics: Movable, Tangible, Ownership does not require land registration 
• Examples: Vehicles, Furniture and appliances, Electronics and tools, Clothing and 
jewelry, Money and investments 
• Relevant Legislation: Sale of Goods Act, Personal Property Security Act (PPSA) 
 
Intellectual Property: Protects creations of the mind rather than physical objects. These rights 
allow creators to control how their work is used and to benefit financially from it. 
• Characteristics: Intangible, Time-limited protection, Governed primarily by federal law 
• Examples: Copyright: books, music, films, digital content, Trademarks: logos, brand 
names, slogans, Patents: inventions and technological processes, Software and apps 
• Relevant Federal Legislation: Copyright Act, Patent Act, Trademarks Act 
 
Historical Definition of Property. The legal definition of property in Canada has evolved 
significantly over time. Early property law focused almost entirely on land ownership, while 
modern law recognizes a wide range of tangible and intangible property rights. These changes 
reflect social, economic, and technological developments. 
 
Early Property Law: Land-Based Ownership 
Feudal and British Roots: Canadian property law is largely based on English common law, 
which developed under a feudal system. Property was viewed as physical landownership, and 
legal protection focused on real property rather than personal possessions. Under this system: 
• All land was technically owned by the Crown

• Individuals held land through grants or tenures 
• Property rights were tied primarily to land, not movable goods 
 
Expansion to Personal Property: As trade and commerce expanded in the 18th and 19th 
centuries: 
• Personal property (goods and chattels) became increasingly valuable 
• The law began recognizing ownership and transfer of movable items 
 
Legislation such as the Sale of Goods Act helped formalize: 
• Ownership of personal property 
• Rights and responsibilities in buying and selling goods 
• Legal remedies when goods were defective or contracts were breached 
 
This marked a shift from land-based wealth to commercial and consumer-based property. 
 
Recognition of Intangible Property 
Intellectual Property Development: With industrialization and technological advancement, the 
law expanded to protect non-physical property: 
• Creative works, Inventions, Brand identity 
Federal legislation introduced legal protections such as: 
• Copyright, Patents, Trademarks 
 
This change reflected the understanding that ideas and creations have economic value, even 
without physical form. 
 
Indigenous Perspectives and Legal Recognition: Historically, Canadian law: 
• Ignored or displaced Indigenous systems of land ownership 
• Treated Indigenous land as Crown land 
Over time, the legal definition of property expanded to recognize: 
• Aboriginal title, Treaty rights, Traditional land use 
 
Section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 affirmed existing Aboriginal and treaty rights, 
significantly altering how property is legally understood in Canada. 
 
Modern Developments: Digital and Electronic Property: In the modern era, property law 
continues to evolve with technology: 
• Digital assets, Electronic contracts, Online intellectual property, Software licences 
 
While these forms may not be owned in the traditional sense, the law recognizes rights of access, 
use, and control, expanding the definition of property beyond physical ownership. 
 
Changes in Who Could Own Property. Historically, the right to own property in Canada was 
limited to a narrow group of people, primarily male British subjects, and was influenced by 
English common law and colonial policies. Married women were generally prohibited from 
owning property independently, as their property was legally controlled by their husbands under 
the doctrine of coverture.

Indigenous peoples were largely excluded from property ownership under Canadian law, as their 
lands were claimed by the Crown and governed through treaties and legislation such as the 
Indian Act. Enslaved persons and many racialized immigrants also faced legal and practical 
barriers to ownership.  
 
Over time, reforms such as the Married Women’s Property Acts, the abolition of slavery, human 
rights legislation, and the constitutional recognition of Indigenous rights in Section 35 of the 
Constitution Act, 1982 expanded property ownership rights. As a result, modern Canadian law 
recognizes the right of individuals, regardless of gender, race, or marital status, to own and 
control property, reflecting broader social and legal commitments to equality and inclusion. 
 
Rights of a Property Owner 
In Canadian law, property ownership is often described as a “bundle of rights.” Ownership does 
not mean unlimited control; instead, it includes several legally recognized rights that may be 
shared, restricted, or regulated by law. 
 
1. Right to Possess and Use Property: An owner has the right to possess and use their 
property in a lawful manner. This includes living in a home, operating a business, or 
using land for permitted purposes. This right is limited by zoning bylaws, environmental 
regulations, and other laws. 
 
2. Right to Quiet Enjoyment: Quiet enjoyment means the owner has the right to use and 
enjoy their property without unreasonable interference from others. This right protects 
owners from trespass, nuisance, or unlawful disturbance, but it does not prevent lawful 
government regulation or the rights of others. 
 
3. Right to Sell or Transfer Property: An owner generally has the right to sell, gift, or 
transfer property to another person. For real property, this transfer must comply with 
formal legal requirements, including written agreements and registration under the Land 
Titles Act. 
 
4. Right to Lease Property: An owner may lease property to another person, granting 
exclusive possession for a fixed period in exchange for rent. While ownership remains 
with the landlord, certain rights and responsibilities transfer to the tenant under 
legislation such as the Residential Tenancies Act. 
 
5. Right to Grant Rights to Third Parties: Owners may grant limited rights to others, 
such as: Easements or rights of way, Licences to use property, Utility access 
These rights reduce exclusive control but allow shared or limited use. 
 
6. Right to Mortgage Property: An owner may use property as security for a loan by 
granting a mortgage or other registered interest. The lender gains certain rights, such as 
the power of sale, if the borrower defaults.

7. Water Rights: Property owners may have limited rights to use water adjacent to or on 
their land, subject to provincial regulation. In Alberta, water use is strictly controlled 
through licensing and does not give absolute ownership of water resources. 
 
8. Air Space Rights: Owners have rights to the air space above their land, but only to a 
reasonable height. These rights are limited by aviation laws, municipal bylaws, and 
public interests. 
 
9. Mineral Rights: Ownership may include mineral rights beneath the land, such as oil, 
gas, or minerals. In many cases in Alberta, mineral rights are owned by the Crown and 
may be separated from surface ownership. 
 
While property owners in Canada enjoy broad rights, those rights are not absolute. Ownership 
consists of a bundle of legally defined rights that can be limited by legislation, shared with 
others, or transferred to third parties.  
 
Other Property Interests 
Not all legal interests in property involve full ownership. Canadian law recognizes several 
limited or shared property interests that grant specific rights or responsibilities without 
transferring complete ownership. These interests help regulate how property is used, controlled, 
or secured. 
 
Lease: A lease is a legal agreement that grants a person (the tenant or lessee) exclusive 
possession of property for a fixed period in exchange for payment (rent). 
• Ownership remains with the landlord (lessor) 
• Tenant gains exclusive use during the lease term 
• Creates legal rights and obligations for both parties 
Examples: Apartment rental, Vehicle lease 
Governing Legislation (Alberta): Residential Tenancies Act 
 
Licence: A licence is permission to use property without exclusive possession or ownership. 
• Does not transfer possession 
• Usually temporary and revocable 
• Creates fewer legal protections than a lease 
Examples: Software licence, Parking permit, Event ticket 
 
Bailment: Bailment occurs when personal property is temporarily transferred from one person 
(the bailor) to another (the bailee) for a specific purpose. 
• Ownership does not transfer 
• The bailee must take reasonable care of the property 
• Property must be returned after the purpose is complete 
Examples: Repair shop holding equipment, Storage unit, Pawn shop 
 
Lien: A lien is a legal right to retain possession of property until a debt is paid. 
• Secures payment for services or materials 
• May allow sale of the property if debt remains unpaid

• Often registered against property title 
Examples: Mechanic’s lien, Builder’s lien, Lender’s lien 
 
Mortgage Holder (Security Interest): A mortgage creates a security interest in real property in 
favour of a lender (mortgagee). 
• Borrower (mortgagor) retains possession 
• Lender has rights if borrower defaults 
• Mortgage is registered on title 
Examples: Conventional mortgage, Home equity line of credit 
 
Easement and Right of Way: An easement is a legal right to use another person’s land for a 
specific purpose. 
• Does not transfer ownership 
• Usually permanent and registered on title 
• Runs with the land 
Examples: Shared driveway, Utility access, Access road to landlocked property 
 
Other property interests allow individuals and organizations to use, access, or secure property 
without full ownership. These interests balance the rights of owners with the needs of tenants, 
lenders, service providers, and the public, ensuring property is used fairly and efficiently under 
Canadian and Alberta law. 
 
Legal Requirements to Purchase and Sell Property.  
The legal requirements for buying and selling property depend on whether the property is real 
estate (real property) or personal property. Because real estate is permanent and high in value, it 
is subject to stricter legal rules than personal property. 
 
1. Purchasing and Selling Real Estate (Real Property): Real estate transactions are 
highly regulated and must follow formal legal procedures. 
Legal Requirements: 
• Written Contract 
• Agreements must be in writing to be enforceable. 
• Verbal agreements are generally not valid for real estate transactions. 
Registration of Ownership 
• Ownership must be registered under the Land Titles Act. 
• Registration provides legal proof of ownership and priority over other claims. 
Disclosure Obligations 
• Sellers must disclose known material defects. 
• Consumer protection laws such as the Fair Trading Act apply to representations 
made during the sale. 
Spousal Consent (Where Applicable) 
• Under the Dower Act, spousal consent may be required for the sale of a 
matrimonial home. 
Completion of Searches 
• Title searches, encumbrances, property tax status, and zoning compliance must be 
reviewed.

Role of Legal Professionals 
• Lawyers handle the transfer of title and trust funds. 
• Realtors must be licensed and follow professional regulations. 
Relevant Legislation: 
• Law of Property Act 
• Land Titles Act 
• Fair Trading Act 
• Dower Act 
 
2. Purchasing and Selling Personal Property: Personal property transactions are 
generally simpler and less formal. 
Legal Requirements: 
• Contract Formation 
• A contract may be written, verbal, or implied. 
• Terms must include agreement on price, description, and transfer of ownership. 
Transfer of Ownership 
• Ownership usually transfers upon payment and delivery. 
• Registration is generally not required (with some exceptions, such as vehicles). 
Condition of Goods 
• The Sale of Goods Act implies certain conditions and warranties, such as goods 
being fit for purpose. 
Consumer Protection 
• The Fair Trading Act protects buyers from unfair or misleading business 
practices. 
Security Interests 
• If personal property is used as collateral, interests may be registered under the 
Personal Property Security Act (PPSA). 
Relevant Legislation: 
• Sale of Goods Act 
• Fair Trading Act 
• Personal Property Security Act 
 
Key Differences Summary 
Real Estate Personal Property 
Written contract required Verbal or written contract allowed 
Title registration required No title registration (generally) 
Extensive legal searches Minimal legal searches 
Governed by land-specific legislation Governed by sales and consumer laws 
Higher legal formality More flexible transactions 
 
Purchasing and selling real estate involves formal contracts, registration, and legal oversight due 
to the permanence and value of land. In contrast, personal property transactions are more 
flexible, with fewer legal requirements, reflecting their movable nature and lower risk.

Understanding these differences helps ensure lawful and informed property transactions in 
Canada. 
 
Legal Requirements to Rent or Lease Property 
Renting or leasing property involves a legal agreement that grants temporary use of property 
without transferring ownership. The legal requirements differ depending on whether the property 
is real estate or personal property, with real estate subject to more extensive regulation. 
 
1. Renting or Leasing Real Estate: Leasing real estate is highly regulated to protect both 
landlords and tenants. 
Legal Requirements: 
• Written Lease Agreement 
• While some leases may be verbal, written agreements are strongly recommended 
and commonly required for clarity and enforcement. 
• The lease must clearly state rent, term, responsibilities, and conditions. 
Compliance with Residential Legislation 
• In Alberta, residential rentals are governed by the Residential Tenancies Act 
(RTA). 
• The RTA sets rules for rent increases, security deposits, entry rights, termination, 
and dispute resolution. 
Security Deposits 
• Landlords may collect security deposits, which must follow legal limits and 
handling requirements under the RTA. 
Landlord and Tenant Obligations 
• Landlords must provide safe, habitable premises. 
• Tenants must pay rent and maintain reasonable care of the property. 
Registration and Property Rights 
• Ownership remains with the landlord and is recorded under the Land Titles Act. 
• Tenants gain exclusive possession for the lease term. 
Consumer Protection 
• The Fair Trading Act prohibits misleading or unfair practices related to rental 
agreements. 
Relevant Legislation: 
• Residential Tenancies Act 
• Fair Trading Act 
• Land Titles Act 
• Law of Property Act 
 
2. Renting or Leasing Personal Property: Leasing personal property is generally less 
regulated and more flexible. 
Legal Requirements: 
• Lease or Rental Agreement 
• Agreements may be written or verbal. 
• Terms typically include duration, payment, use restrictions, and return conditions. 
Condition and Use of Goods 
• Under the Sale of Goods Act, leased items must be fit for their intended purpose.

• The renter must use the property as agreed and return it in acceptable condition. 
Security Interests 
• If the leased property is used as collateral or financed, interests may be registered 
under the Personal Property Security Act (PPSA). 
Consumer Protection 
• The Fair Trading Act applies to rental businesses and protects consumers from 
unfair practices. 
Transfer of Possession 
• Possession transfers temporarily, but ownership remains with the lessor. 
Relevant Legislation: 
• Sale of Goods Act 
• Personal Property Security Act 
• Fair Trading Act 
 
Key Differences Summary 
Real Estate Leasing Personal Property Leasing 
Governed by Residential Tenancies Act Governed by Sale of Goods Act 
Strong tenant protections Fewer statutory protections 
Strict rules on deposits and termination Flexible contract terms 
Exclusive possession of property Temporary possession of goods 
Highly regulated Less regulated 
 
Leasing real estate involves strict legal requirements to protect housing stability and safety, while 
leasing personal property focuses on contractual terms and consumer protection.  
 
Implications of Assignment and Subletting. Assignment and subletting occur when a tenant 
transfers occupancy rights to another person. While both involve third parties, they carry 
different legal implications for the tenant, landlord, and new occupant. 
 
Assignment: An assignment occurs when a tenant transfers all remaining rights and 
responsibilities under a lease to another person (the assignee). Legal Implications: 
• Tenant Responsibility Ends: The original tenant is usually released from the lease once 
the assignment is complete, unless the lease states otherwise. 
• Landlord Consent Required: Most leases require the landlord’s written consent before an 
assignment can occur. 
• New Tenant Takes Over: The assignee becomes fully responsible for rent, damages, and 
lease terms. 
• Lease Continues Unchanged: The original lease terms remain in effect; only the tenant 
changes. 
 
Subletting: A sublet occurs when a tenant rents the property to another person while remaining 
legally responsible to the landlord. Legal Implications: 
• Original Tenant Remains Liable: The tenant remains responsible for rent, damages, and 
lease compliance. 
• Temporary Arrangement: Sublets usually last for part of the lease term.

• Landlord Approval Often Required: Many leases and the Residential Tenancies Act 
require landlord consent. 
• Separate Agreement: A new contract exists between the tenant and subtenant, but the 
landlord is not part of it. 
 
Electronic and Internet transactions have significantly changed how property and commercial 
agreements are formed in Canada, creating new legal considerations for buyers and sellers. 
Canadian law recognizes electronic contracts and electronic signatures as legally binding, 
provided there is clear intent, consent, and the ability to authenticate the parties involved. 
However, these transactions raise concerns related to identity verification, fraud, privacy, and 
data security, particularly when agreements are completed online without face-to-face 
interaction.  
 
Disclosure requirements, consumer protection laws, and fair trading legislation continue to apply 
to electronic transactions, meaning misleading representations or unfair practices remain 
unlawful regardless of the medium used. As a result, while electronic and Internet transactions 
increase efficiency and accessibility, they also require careful attention to security, accuracy, and 
legal compliance to ensure agreements are enforceable and rights are protected. 
 
Listing Property. The procedures involved in listing a property for sale follow a structured legal 
and professional process designed to protect both the seller and potential buyers. The property 
owner typically begins by selecting a licensed real estate professional, who conducts a market 
analysis to determine an appropriate listing price based on comparable properties and current 
market conditions.  
 
The seller and realtor then enter into a written listing agreement that outlines the listing price, 
commission, duration of the listing, and the responsibilities of each party. Before the property is 
marketed, the seller must ensure accurate disclosure of material facts about the property, 
including known defects or restrictions.  
 
Once listed, the property is advertised through multiple platforms, showings are arranged, and 
offers are presented to the seller. Throughout the process, legal and ethical obligations apply, 
including compliance with consumer protection legislation and real estate regulations, until an 
acceptable offer is received and the property moves toward sale. 
 
Offer to Purchase. An offer to purchase is a legally binding proposal made by a buyer to buy 
property under specific terms. To be enforceable, it must clearly outline the rights and 
obligations of both the buyer and the seller.  
 
Real estate transactions, an offer to purchase typically includes the following elements. 
• The offer identifies the parties involved, including the legal names of the buyer and 
seller, and provides a legal description of the property to ensure there is no uncertainty 
about what is being purchased. It states the purchase price and the amount of the deposit, 
which demonstrates the buyer’s seriousness and is usually held in trust. The offer also 
specifies the possession or closing date, indicating when ownership and possession will 
transfer.

• A key element of an offer to purchase is the inclusion of subject-to conditions, which 
protect the buyer or seller by making the agreement conditional upon certain 
requirements being met. Common conditions include subject to financing approval, 
subject to a satisfactory home inspection, subject to the sale of the buyer’s current 
property, or subject to review by a lawyer. These conditions must be satisfied or waived 
within a stated time period; otherwise, the offer may become void. 
 
• Additional elements may include adjustments for property taxes or utilities, included or 
excluded items, and the method of acceptance. Once all terms are agreed and conditions 
are met or waived, the offer becomes a binding purchase contract enforceable by law. 
 
Legal Search. When purchasing real property, several legal and practical searches are required 
to properly investigate the property and protect the buyer’s interests. These searches help identify 
potential legal, financial, or physical issues before the sale is completed. 
 
• Title search is conducted to confirm legal ownership and to identify any registered 
encumbrances such as mortgages, liens, caveats, or easements under the Land Titles Act. 
This ensures the seller has the right to sell the property and reveals any third-party 
interests that may affect ownership. 
 
• Property tax search confirms that municipal taxes are paid and up to date. Outstanding 
taxes can become the responsibility of the new owner if not addressed prior to closing. 
 
• Zoning and land-use search verifies that the property complies with municipal zoning 
bylaws and identifies permitted uses, building restrictions, or non-conforming uses that 
could limit future development or renovations. 
 
• Compliance or development search checks whether buildings and improvements were 
constructed with proper permits and approvals. This can reveal illegal structures or 
unapproved renovations. 
 
• Survey or Real Property Report (RPR) confirms property boundaries, location of 
structures, and encroachments onto neighbouring land or municipal property. 
 
Additional searches may include utility searches, environmental assessments, or condominium 
document reviews, depending on the type of property.  
 
Financing. When purchasing property, buyers may choose between a cash sale or financing the 
purchase. Each option has different legal and financial implications that affect risk, cost, and 
ownership obligations. 
 
• Cash sale occurs when the buyer pays the full purchase price without borrowing money. 
Because no lender is involved, there is no mortgage registered against the property, 
which simplifies the transaction and reduces legal fees and interest costs. Cash buyers are 
not subject to lender approval, making the purchase faster and often more attractive to

sellers. However, the buyer must have sufficient funds available and assumes full 
financial risk. 
 
• Financed purchase involves borrowing money from a lender and using the property as 
security. A conventional mortgage is granted when the buyer provides a down payment 
of at least 20 percent of the purchase price. The lender registers a mortgage on title, and 
the borrower (mortgagor) agrees to repay the loan with interest over time. 
 
• CMHC high-ratio mortgage applies when the down payment is less than 20 percent. 
Because this type of mortgage presents greater risk to the lender, it must be insured by 
the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC). The cost of insurance is added 
to the mortgage, increasing the total amount owed by the buyer. 
 
• Home equity line of credit (HELOC) allows a property owner to borrow against the 
equity they have built in their home. The loan is secured against the property and offers 
flexible borrowing and repayment, but it increases debt and places the property at risk if 
payments are not made. Each financing option involves trade-offs between flexibility, 
cost, and risk. 
 
Mortgage relationship. The mortgagee and the mortgagor have distinct but interrelated rights 
and obligations under Canadian and Alberta property law. 
 
Mortgagor is the borrower and legal owner of the property. The mortgagor has the right to 
possess, use, and enjoy the property, including renting or selling it, provided the terms of the 
mortgage are followed. The mortgagor’s primary obligations are to make mortgage payments as 
agreed, maintain the property, pay property taxes and insurance, and comply with all mortgage 
conditions. Failure to meet these obligations may place the mortgagor in default. 
 
Mortgagee is the lender, typically a bank or financial institution, that holds a registered interest 
in the property as security for the loan. The mortgagee has the right to receive regular payments, 
charge interest, and enforce the mortgage if the mortgagor defaults. Enforcement rights may 
include demanding payment, initiating foreclosure or power of sale proceedings, or taking 
possession of the property in accordance with legislation. The mortgagee is obligated to act in 
good faith, discharge the mortgage once the debt is fully repaid, and follow legal procedures 
when enforcing its rights. 
 
The mortgagor retains ownership and use of the property but assumes ongoing financial and 
maintenance responsibilities, while the mortgagee holds a secured interest designed to protect the 
repayment of the loan. 
 
Professionals in buying and selling. The buying and selling of real property involves several 
professionals, each with a specific role to ensure the transaction is legal, accurate, and informed.  
 
• Realtors act as intermediaries between buyers and sellers by marketing properties, 
arranging showings, negotiating offers, and ensuring disclosure obligations are met in 
accordance with real estate regulations.

• Lawyers provide legal advice, draft and review contracts, conduct title searches, register 
transfers and mortgages, and ensure that funds are properly transferred on closing.  
• Assessors determine the assessed value of a property for taxation purposes, which helps 
municipalities calculate property taxes and allows buyers to understand ongoing tax 
obligations.  
• Surveyors prepare surveys or Real Property Reports that identify property boundaries, 
improvements, encroachments, and rights of way, helping prevent boundary disputes.  
• Property inspectors examine the physical condition of the property, identifying 
structural, mechanical, or safety issues that may affect value or lead to future repair costs.  
 
Remedies for breach of contract. When a real estate purchase contract is breached, the law 
provides several remedies to address the harm caused and, where possible, enforce the 
agreement.  
• Specific performance, where a court orders the breaching party to complete the 
transaction as agreed. This remedy is often sought in real estate cases because each 
property is considered unique.  
• Damages, which involve monetary compensation to cover losses suffered by the non-
breaching party, such as the difference between the contract price and a later sale price, 
legal costs, or additional expenses incurred due to the breach.  
• Forfeiture of the deposit may occur if the buyer breaches the contract, allowing the 
seller to retain the deposit as compensation, subject to court review for fairness.  
• Terminate or rescind the contract, in some cases, the innocent party may also have the 
right to release both parties from further obligations.

LGS3020: DISPUTE RESOLUTION 
 
Description: Students examine and apply methods such as negotiation, mediation, arbitration, 
adjudication and litigation, and identify challenging issues related to the dispute resolution 
methods. 
 
Why Dispute Resolution Matters. Conflict is part of everyday life, at work, at school, in 
families, and in communities. In Canada and Alberta, there are structured ways to resolve 
disputes that aim to be fair, safe, and lawful.  
 
Benefits of Different Dispute Resolution Methods 
Negotiation allows the people involved in a dispute to talk directly and try to reach an agreement 
on their own. Negotiation works best when both sides are willing to cooperate and communicate 
respectfully. Benefits of negotiation include: 
• It is informal and easy to access 
• It usually costs little or no money

LGS3040: NEGLIGENCE 
 
Description: Students explore the legal meaning of negligence and legal actions relating to 
negligence. Negligence is one of the most significant areas of civil law in Canada. Students will 
explore how courts determine responsibility for harm, how liability is assessed, and how 
remedies are awarded through the civil justice system. 
 
What Constitutes Negligence? Evolution of Negligence. Negligence developed through 
common law, primarily in England, and was adopted into Canadian law. Early legal systems 
focused on intentional harm; negligence law emerged to address unintentional but careless 
conduct. 
 
Evolution of the Legal Area of Negligence 
1. Origins in Common Law 
o Negligence law developed from English common law, which initially focused on 
intentional wrongdoing and property damage. 
o Early courts did not recognize liability for careless acts unless there was a 
contractual relationship or direct harm to property. 
2. Industrial Revolution and Social Change 
o With industrialization, workplaces and public spaces became more hazardous. 
o Accidents increased, and society recognized the need for legal protections for 
individuals harmed by others’ carelessness. 
o Courts began to consider duty of care beyond contractual obligations. 
3. The Neighbour Principle (1932) 
o Landmark case: Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932), UK. 
o Established that individuals owe a duty to take reasonable care to avoid acts that 
could foreseeably harm “neighbours” — those closely affected by one’s actions. 
o This principle became the foundation of modern negligence law in Canada. 
4. Adoption in Canadian Law 
o Canadian courts gradually adopted common law principles, refining them to 
reflect Canadian values and legislation. 
o Courts started recognizing duties in diverse contexts: medical, educational, 
professional services, and product liability. 
5. Modern Canadian Negligence Law 
o Today, negligence law in Canada is well-established and adaptable. 
o Courts weigh elements such as duty of care, standard of care, breach, causation, 
and damages. 
o Legislation in Alberta and across Canada, such as the Occupiers’ Liability Act, 
also shapes liability alongside common law. 
6. Ongoing Development 
o Courts continue to refine negligence principles in response to: 
▪ Emerging technologies (e.g., self-driving vehicles) 
▪ Health care and professional accountability 
▪ Environmental and consumer protection concerns

Negligence law evolved from a narrow focus on intentional harm to a broader principle 
recognizing society’s interest in preventing careless acts that harm others. Its modern form 
combines judicial precedent with statutory guidance to protect individuals while balancing 
fairness and reasonableness. 
 
Elements of Negligence. To succeed in a negligence claim, a plaintiff must prove four elements 
on a balance of probabilities. Failure to prove any one of the elements result in the claim failing. 
1. Duty of care existed 
2. Standard of care was breached 
3. Causation between breach and harm 
4. Damages resulted 
 
Duty of Care 
The Neighbour Principle. Established in Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932), states: Individuals 
must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which they can reasonably foresee would 
likely injure their “neighbour.” A neighbour is defined as anyone closely and directly affected by 
one’s actions. Canadian courts apply this principle to determine whether a duty of care exists. 
 
Rise to Duty of Care. Courts consider proximity, foreseeability, and public policy when 
determining whether a duty of care exists. Common duty of care relationships include: 
• Drivers to other road users 
• Teachers to students 
• Doctors to patients 
• Manufacturers to consumers 
• Property owners to visitors 
 
Standard of Care 
The Reasonable Person & Foreseeability. The reasonable person standard asks: What would 
an ordinary, prudent person have done in the same circumstances? Foreseeability refers to 
whether a reasonable person would anticipate that harm could result from their actions. 
 
Special Categories. The standard of care may be adjusted for: 
• Minors: Compared to children of similar age and experience 
• Professionals: Compared to reasonably competent professionals in the same field 
• Experts: Held to higher standards due to specialized knowledge 
 
Breach of Standard of Care. A breach occurs when conduct falls below the expected standard. 
Courts assess: Risk of harm, Severity of potential injury, Cost and practicality of precautions. 
 
Causation 
Link Between Breach and Damage. In negligence, it is not enough to show that a duty of care 
existed and that the standard of care was breached. The plaintiff must also prove that the 
defendant’s breach actually caused the harm or damage suffered. This connection is causation. 
 
Proximate Cause 
• The breach must be the proximate cause of the harm.

CTS: Legal Studies 30 (7 credits) 
 
Page | 22 
• Proximate cause asks whether the harm was a direct and reasonably foreseeable result of 
the defendant’s actions. 
• Courts often apply the “but-for” test: “But for the defendant’s breach, would the harm 
have occurred?” 
• If the answer is no, the breach is a cause of the damage. 
• If the harm would have occurred regardless of the breach, the link is broken, and the 
claim fails. 
 
Foreseeability 
• Courts consider whether a reasonable person could have foreseen the harm resulting from 
the breach. 
• If the harm was too remote or unexpected, the defendant may not be liable, even if there 
was a breach. 
 
Multiple Causes 
• Sometimes, more than one factor contributes to the damage. 
• Courts may apportion liability among multiple defendants or consider contributory 
negligence if the plaintiff partially caused the harm. 
• Liability is assessed on the balance of probabilities (more likely than not). 
 
Examples: 
• A driver runs a red light (breach) and hits a pedestrian, causing injury (damage). 
• The driver’s breach directly caused the injury and the harm was foreseeable. 
• If a freak event, like a meteorite, also caused the injury at the same time, the court would 
evaluate proximate cause and may limit liability. 
 
The link between breach and damage ensures that negligence liability is fair and reasonable. The 
defendant is only responsible for harm that was directly caused and reasonably foreseeable from 
their breach of duty. 
 
Multiple Causes 
• Apportionment of Liability. When multiple defendants contribute to harm, courts may 
divide responsibility among them. 
• Balance of Probabilities. The plaintiff must show it is more likely than not that the 
defendant’s conduct caused the damage. 
• Contributory Negligence. If the plaintiff contributed to their own harm, damages may 
be reduced proportionally under Alberta legislation. 
 
Damages and Remedies 
Loss or Injury. Actual harm must be proven. This may include: Physical injury, Psychological 
harm, Property damage, & Financial loss. 
 
Types of Damages 
• General damages: Pain and suffering 
• Special damages: Medical bills, lost income 
• Punitive damages: Rare; intended to punish egregious conduct

Civil Court Structure and Process (Alberta) 
Structure and Process of the Civil Court in Alberta. Civil law in Alberta deals with disputes 
between individuals, organizations, or both, usually over money, property, or rights. Negligence 
claims are handled in civil courts, primarily the Provincial Court of Alberta and the Court of 
Kings’s Bench. 
 
Court Structure 
1. Provincial Court of Alberta – Civil Division 
o Handles claims up to $100,000 (as of current legislation). 
o Faster and less formal than higher courts. 
o Small claims and straightforward negligence cases are usually heard here. 
2. Court of Kings’s Bench of Alberta 
o Handles claims over $100,000, complex cases, and appeals from Provincial Court. 
o More formal procedures; allows for expert testimony and detailed discovery. 
3. Court of Appeal of Alberta 
o Reviews decisions from the Court of Queen’s Bench or Provincial Court. 
o Focuses on errors of law, not re-assessing facts unless there is a clear mistake. 
 
Civil Court Process 
1. Initiating a Claim (Plaintiff’s Role) 
o Civil Claim Form: The plaintiff sets out the basis of the claim, including facts, 
legal basis, and damages sought. 
o Service of Claim: The claim must be formally delivered to the defendant. 
o Supporting Documents: Affidavits, contracts, or evidence supporting the claim. 
2. Defending a Claim (Defendant’s Role) 
o Dispute Note or Statement of Defence: The defendant responds to the plaintiff’s 
claim, accepting, denying, or providing alternative facts. 
o Counterclaims: Defendants may assert their own claims against the plaintiff. 
o Evidence Submission: Supporting documents or affidavits are provided. 
3. Discovery Phase 
o Both parties exchange relevant information. 
o Includes interrogatories, document production, and depositions. 
o Helps clarify issues and avoids surprises at trial. 
4. Pre-Trial and Settlement Discussions 
o Courts often encourage settlement before trial. 
o Mediation or negotiation may reduce time, cost, and stress.

5. Trial 
o Both sides present evidence and arguments. 
o Witnesses, including expert witnesses, may be called. 
o Court decides liability and awards damages if applicable. 
6. Judgment and Enforcement 
o Judgment: Court orders who is liable and the amount owed. 
o Enforcement Methods: Wage garnishment, Seizure of property, Payment orders 
or liens 
7. Appeals 
o Parties can appeal decisions based on errors of law or procedure. 
o Appellate courts review the legal reasoning, not usually the facts. 
 
Civil courts use “balance of probabilities” rather than “beyond a reasonable doubt.” Documents 
and procedural steps are crucial; errors may lead to delays or dismissal. Understanding court 
structure and process helps plaintiffs and defendants navigate claims effectively. 
 
Special Types of Negligence 
Voluntary Assumption of Risk. This defence applies when a person knowingly accepts the risk 
of harm. 
 
Special Situations and Types of Liability. While general negligence requires proving duty, 
breach, causation, and damages, certain situations impose liability automatically or in a special 
way. These are designed to protect the public, ensure accountability, or allocate risk fairly. 
 
Strict Liability: Liability imposed regardless of fault or intent. The defendant is responsible for 
harm even if they took all reasonable care. Protects the public from inherently dangerous 
activities where the risk cannot be fully eliminated. Common Situations: 
• Ultra-hazardous activities (e.g., blasting, keeping wild animals) 
• Product liability in some consumer cases 
 
Vicarious Liability: Liability imposed on one person for the actions of another. Employers held 
responsible for employees acting within the scope of employment. Ensures that victims can 
recover damages from parties with the resources to pay and encourages organizations to 
supervise employees properly. 
• Example: A delivery driver negligently causes an accident while performing work duties; 
the employer may be liable. 
 
Occupiers’ Liability: Responsibility of property owners or occupiers to ensure visitors are 
reasonably safe. Applies to all lawful visitors (invitees, licensees, and in some cases, trespassers). 
Duty includes keeping premises in a safe condition, warning of hazards, and taking reasonable 
precautions. Governed by statutes like Alberta’s Occupiers’ Liability Act. 
• Example: A store owner must ensure wet floors are cleaned or marked with warning 
signs to prevent slip and fall accidents. 
 
Waivers: Legal documents where a person agrees to accept risks and relinquishes the right to 
sue for negligence. Must be clear, unambiguous, and voluntarily signed. Cannot waive liability

organizations accountable for their employees’ actions (vicarious liability), ensure safety on 
private property (occupiers’ liability), Allow voluntary risk acceptance while clarifying legal 
responsibility (waivers). Understanding these situations helps students recognize when

What Is a Controversial Issue?  
A controversial issue is a topic, event, or situation that: 
1. Involves strongly differing opinions – People or groups have conflicting views about 
what is right, fair, or acceptable. 
2. Raises ethical, moral, social, or legal questions – The topic often challenges values, 
beliefs, or established rules. 
3. Generates public debate or discussion – Controversial issues usually provoke discussion

4. Has legal or societal implications – Decisions or policies about the issue may affect laws,

A controversial issue is not simply a matter of personal preference; it affects society or law in 
some way. Understanding different viewpoints is essential before proposing solutions. Many 
controversial issues evolve over time as laws, social norms, and public opinions change.

certain circumstances.

facts.

the law, & allows the law to evolve gradually over time.

Actus Reus (The Guilty Act): The physical component of a crime; the voluntary action, 
omission, or conduct that constitutes the criminal offence. 
o Must be a voluntary act or omission that breaches the law. 
o Includes acts such as assault, theft, or driving while impaired. 
o In some crimes, omission (failing to act when there is a legal duty) can also 
constitute actus reus. 
 
Mens Rea (The Guilty Mind): The mental component of a crime; the intention or knowledge of 
wrongdoing. 
o Shows that the accused had criminal intent, recklessness, or knowledge that their 
conduct was wrongful. 
o Different levels of mens rea include: 
▪ Intention: Deliberate purpose to commit the crime. 
▪ Knowledge: Awareness that one’s actions are likely to cause harm. 
▪ Recklessness: Conscious disregard for a substantial risk. 
▪ Criminal negligence: Failure to meet a reasonable standard of care that 
results in harm. 
 
Additional Elements (Context-Specific) 
• Causation: The actus reus must cause the prohibited consequence (e.g., in homicide, the 
action must cause death). 
• Concurrence: Actus reus and mens rea must occur together, the guilty mind must 
coincide with the guilty act. 
 
Offences are classified based on their seriousness and procedure, which determines how they are

offences, and indictable offences.  
 
Summary Offences (Including Provincial): Minor offences, often less serious in nature.

• Penalties: Range from summary-level fines or jail to indictable-level imprisonment. 
• Examples: Assault causing bodily harm, theft under $5,000, mischief. 
 
Indictable Offences: Serious criminal offences with the most severe penalties. Tried in Court of 
King’s Bench, often before a judge or jury. Includes preliminary inquiry (to assess evidence). 
Trial may be judge-alone or judge-and-jury.

Powers of the police are defined by the Criminal Code of Canada, the Charter of Rights and 
Freedoms, and provincial statutes. Police have the authority to enforce the law, maintain public 
safety, and investigate offences, but their powers are limited by legal safeguards to protect 
individual rights.  
 
Arrest: Taking a person into custody because they are suspected of committing an offence. 
• Powers and Requirements: 
o Police can arrest with or without a warrant depending on the circumstances. 
o Must have reasonable grounds to believe an offence has been committed. 
o Must inform the individual of the reason for the arrest. 
 
Questioning (Interrogation): Police may question individuals to gather information about an 
offence. 
• Rules and Limits: 
o Individuals have the right to remain silent (Charter Section 7 & 11(c)). 
o Must be informed of the right to counsel (Charter Section 10(b)). 
o Police cannot use threats, deception, or coercion to obtain a statement. 
 
Search and Seizure: Police may search a person, place, or thing to find evidence of a crime. 
• Limits and Safeguards: 
o Must have reasonable grounds to believe evidence of an offence is present. 
o For most searches, a warrant issued by a judge is required. 
o Some warrantless searches are allowed (e.g., during arrest or for public safety). 
o Evidence obtained unlawfully may be excluded in court (Charter Section 24(2)). 
 
Custody (Detention): Holding a person in police custody for investigation or until they are 
charged. Ensure the individual does not flee, destroy evidence, or pose a threat to public safety. 
• Rights of Individuals in Custody: 
o Right to be informed of the reason for detention. 
o Right to legal counsel. 
o Right to be free from cruel or unusual treatment (Charter Section 12).

The Charter of Rights and Freedoms guarantee specific rights to individuals who are arrested 
or detained to protect them from abuse of state power and to ensure a fair criminal process. 
These rights are primarily found in Sections 7, 9, 10, and 11 of the Charter.  
 
Right to Be Informed of the Reason for Arrest or Detention (Section 10(a)): Individuals 
must be immediately informed of the reason they are being arrested or detained. This ensures the 
accused understands the nature of the alleged offence. 
 
Right to Legal Counsel (Section 10(b)): Individuals have the right to consult a lawyer without 
delay and to have a lawyer present during questioning. Police must inform the person of this 
right and allow access to legal advice. 
 
Right to Remain Silent (Section 7 & Common Law): Individuals are protected from self-
incrimination. They may refuse to answer questions until they have consulted legal counsel. 
 
Right to Habeas Corpus (Section 7 & Section 24): Individuals cannot be detained arbitrarily. 
They may challenge unlawful detention in court to secure release. 
 
Right to Be Free from Unreasonable Search and Seizure (Section 8): Individuals have the 
right to privacy in their person, home, and possessions. Evidence obtained through illegal search 
or seizure may be excluded from court. 
 
Right to Be Tried Within a Reasonable Time (Section 11(b)) Individuals charged with an 
offence are entitled to a speedy trial. Prevents indefinite detention without resolution. 
 
Right to Fair Trial and Due Process (Sections 11(d)–(f)): Right to presumption of innocence 
until proven guilty. Right to confront witnesses and obtain a fair hearing. Right to protection 
against cruel or unusual punishment (Section 12). 
 
Bail hearing is a court proceeding held shortly after an individual is arrested to determine 
whether they should be released from custody pending trial and under what conditions, such as 
reporting to a bail supervisor or surrendering travel documents. Its purpose is to balance the 
presumption of innocence with public safety and the risk that the accused may flee, re-offend, or 
interfere with the administration of justice. 
 
Preliminary hearing is a procedural step in the criminal process for serious indictable offences, 
where a Provincial Court judge reviews the evidence presented by the Crown to determine 
whether there is sufficient evidence to proceed to trial. It acts as a safeguard to prevent 
unnecessary trials and ensures that the accused’s case is supported by credible evidence before it 
reaches the superior court. 
 
The Crown counsel (prosecutor) represents the public interest and the state in prosecuting 
criminal offences. Their role is to present evidence, question witnesses, and make legal 
arguments to prove the accused’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, while also ensuring that the 
trial is conducted fairly and in accordance with the law.

The defence counsel represents the accused individual, protecting their legal rights and 
challenging the Crown’s evidence. The defence may present evidence, cross-examine witnesses, 
and make legal arguments to create reasonable doubt or assert applicable defences.  
 
A criminal trial can be conducted either as a trial by judge alone or as a trial by judge and 
jury, depending on the offence and the accused’s choice.  
 
• Trial by judge alone, the judge serves as both the arbiter of law and the finder of fact, 
deciding guilt and delivering the sentence. This option is often chosen for complex cases 
involving technical or legal issues where a jury may find the law difficult to navigate.  
• Trial by judge and jury, the judge oversees legal procedures and instructs the jury on 
the law, while the jury of citizens determines the facts and delivers a verdict of guilty or 
not guilty. This type of trial is typically reserved for more serious indictable offences and 
emphasizes public participation in the justice system.  
 
Jury selection process is designed to ensure that juries are composed of impartial citizens who 
can fairly decide a case. Potential jurors are randomly selected from the provincial or territorial 
voters’ list, health card registries, or other government databases. Once summoned, individuals 
undergo a process called voir dire, where the Crown, defence, and judge can question jurors to 
determine if they have bias, conflicts of interest, or inability to serve impartially.  
 
Both the Crown and defence are allowed a limited number of challenges to exclude certain 
jurors, either for cause (specific reason) or peremptory challenges (no reason needed, where 
allowed). From this pool, typically 12 jurors are selected for criminal trials, with additional 
alternates in case a juror cannot continue. The final jury is intended to represent a cross-section 
of the community and decide the facts of the case independently of the judge. 
 
The onus and burden of proof define who must prove a case and to what standard.  
• The onus refers to the responsibility of a party to establish a fact or issue in a legal 
proceeding. 
• Burden of proof specifies the level of certainty required to meet that responsibility.  
• In criminal trials, the Crown (prosecution) bears the burden of proof, meaning it must 
prove the accused’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, the highest standard in law, 
reflecting the seriousness of depriving someone of liberty.  
 
The accused generally has no obligation to prove innocence, although they may bear the burden 
of establishing certain defences or exceptions on a balance of probabilities basis (e.g., self-
defence). This system ensures the presumption of innocence is maintained and protects 
individuals from wrongful conviction. 
 
Admissibility and reliability of evidence are central to ensuring a fair trial.  
• Hearsay: A statement made outside of court that is offered to prove the truth of its 
content. Hearsay is generally inadmissible because the original speaker cannot be cross-
examined, which may affect reliability. Exceptions: Certain circumstances, such as dying 
declarations or statements against interest, may allow hearsay evidence.

• Prior Bad Acts / Character Evidence: Evidence of the accused’s past wrongdoings or 
criminal history. Such evidence can prejudice the jury by suggesting the accused has a 
criminal disposition. Admissibility: Only allowed if it is directly relevant to an issue in 
the case (e.g., intent, motive, or pattern of behaviour). 
 
• Expert Evidence: Testimony from qualified experts to assist the court in understanding 
technical or scientific matters. The expert’s qualifications, methodology, and relevance 
must be established to ensure reliability. 
 
• Physical and Documentary Evidence: Tangible items (weapons, clothing, DNA) or 
documents (contracts, records) presented at trial. Must be collected, preserved, and 
presented lawfully to avoid challenges of tampering or contamination. 
 
• Charter Considerations: Evidence obtained in violation of the Charter of Rights and 
Freedoms (e.g., illegal search and seizure) may be excluded under Section 24(2) if 
admitting it would bring the administration of justice into disrepute. 
 
Defences. An accused may raise defences to challenge criminal liability, justify their actions, or 
reduce culpability. Defences can be divided into several categories: 
 
Complete Defences. If successful, result in a not guilty verdict. 
• Self-Defence: Using reasonable force to protect oneself or others from imminent harm. 
Force must be proportional to the threat. Cannot be used to retaliate after the fact. 
• Not Criminally Responsible (NCR) – Mental Disorder: The accused was suffering 
from a mental disorder that prevented understanding the nature or wrongfulness of their 
act. Determined through psychiatric evaluation. May result in treatment orders rather than 
traditional punishment. 
• Automatism: The accused’s actions were involuntary due to a physical condition (e.g., 
seizure, sleepwalking). Can negate actus reus. Must be proven on a balance of 
probabilities. 
• Duress: Committing an offence because of a threat of immediate harm. Threat must be 
serious and imminent. No safe avenue of escape. 
 
Partial or Mitigating Defences. These do not result in acquittal but may reduce the severity of 
charges or sentencing. 
• Provocation: A sudden loss of self-control in response to provocative conduct by 
another. May reduce murder to manslaughter. 
• Intoxication: Voluntary or involuntary impairment of mental faculties. Rarely a 
complete defence; may affect specific intent crimes.

• Consent: The alleged victim agreed to the conduct. Consent is not valid for serious 
crimes like sexual assault involving minors or aggravated assault. 
• Mistake of Fact: Honest belief in a set of facts that, if true, would make the act non-
criminal. Must be honest and reasonable.

Criminal justice system includes several alternatives to traditional court proceedings that focus 
on rehabilitation, accountability, and repairing harm rather than punishment. These alternatives 
are commonly used for youth, first-time offenders, and less serious offences.

• Emphasize rehabilitation and reintegration of young offenders. 
• Encourage the use of warnings, cautions, referrals to community programs, and 
conferences instead of formal court proceedings. 
• Aim to hold youth accountable in a manner appropriate to their age and maturity. 
 
Extrajudicial Measures and Sanctions 
• Applied primarily to youth but also available to adults in some circumstances. 
• Include community service, apology letters, counselling, or educational programs. 
• Used when court proceedings are not necessary to protect the public. 
 
Aboriginal or Indigenous Justice Programs and Councils 
• Incorporate traditional Indigenous values and practices, such as sentencing circles or 
community councils. 
• Focus on restorative justice, healing, and reconciliation. 
• Often used where both the victim and offender consent to participation. 
 
Adult Alternative Measures (Diversion Programs) 
• Available for adults charged with minor or first-time offences. 
• May include restitution, community service, counselling, or treatment programs.

Sentencing. Courts may impose a range of sentences depending on the seriousness of the 
offence, the offender’s background, and the goals of sentencing.  
 
• Sentences can include absolute or conditional discharges, where the offender is found 
guilty but no conviction is registered if conditions are met; fines, requiring payment to 
the court; and probation, which allows the offender to remain in the community under 
court-ordered conditions.  
• More serious offences may result in custodial sentences, served in a provincial jail 
(sentences under two years) or a federal penitentiary (sentences of two years or more).

• Courts may also order conditional sentences (house arrest with strict conditions), 
community service, restitution to victims, or suspended sentences combined with 
probation.  
 
Mitigating and aggravating factors are circumstances that influence the severity of a sentence 
by helping the judge determine the offender’s level of responsibility and the appropriate 
punishment.  
 
Mitigating factors reduce the severity of a sentence and may include the offender’s lack of a 
prior criminal record, expressions of remorse, cooperation with police, youth or advanced age, 
mental health issues, or evidence of rehabilitation.  
 
Aggravating factors, increase the severity of a sentence and may include the use of violence or 
a weapon, targeting a vulnerable victim, committing the offence while on probation or parole, 
hate motivation, or a significant prior criminal record. The presence of aggravating factors can 
lead to longer jail terms, stricter probation conditions, or higher fines, while mitigating factors 
may result in reduced penalties, alternative sentences, or greater emphasis on rehabilitation. 
 
Federal penitentiaries and provincial jails serve different roles within the correctional system, 
primarily based on the length of an offender’s sentence and the type of custody required. Federal 
penitentiaries, operated by the Correctional Service of Canada, house offenders sentenced to 
two years or more and focus on long-term incarceration, rehabilitation programs, education, 
treatment, and preparation for eventual reintegration into society.  
 
Provincial jails, operated by provincial governments, hold offenders sentenced to less than two 
years, individuals awaiting trial, those in custody for bail hearings, and offenders serving short-
term sentences. Provincial facilities tend to emphasize short-term detention and supervision, 
while federal institutions place greater emphasis on structured rehabilitation and gradual 
conditional release. 
 
Temporary absence programs, parole, and statutory release are all forms of conditional 
release, but they differ in purpose, timing, and level of supervision.  
• A temporary absence (TA) program allows an offender to leave a correctional facility 
for a short, specific period, for example, to attend treatment, education, employment, 
medical appointments, or family matters—while still serving their sentence and 
remaining under strict supervision.  
• Parole is a conditional release that allows an offender to serve the remainder of their 
sentence in the community under supervision after demonstrating rehabilitation; it may 
be day parole (returning to a facility at night) or full parole (living in the community).  
• Statutory release occurs automatically after an offender has served two-thirds of their 
sentence, unless the National Parole Board determines the offender poses an undue risk to 
public safety; it is not earned in the same way as parole but still includes supervision and 
conditions. 
 
The granting of conditional release is determined by several key factors, including the risk to 
public safety, the seriousness of the offence, the offender’s behaviour while incarcerated,

National Parole Board of Canada, now known as the Parole Board of Canada, is an 
independent administrative tribunal responsible for making decisions about the conditional 
release of federal offenders. Its role is to assess whether an offender can be safely released into 
the community without posing an undue risk to public safety.  
 
The Board reviews information such as the seriousness of the offence, the offender’s criminal 
history, behaviour while incarcerated, participation in rehabilitation programs, and victim impact 
statements. It has the authority to grant, deny, cancel, or revoke parole, impose release 
conditions, and make decisions regarding statutory release and record suspensions.  
 
Youth are treated differently than adults in the criminal justice system because of their stage of 
development, capacity for change, and the long-term impact that criminal convictions can have 
on their future. Research and legal principles recognize that young people are generally less 
mature, more susceptible to peer influence, and less able to fully understand the consequences of 
their actions than adults. As a result, the justice system places greater emphasis on rehabilitation, 
reintegration, and accountability in a developmentally appropriate manner, rather than 
punishment alone. Treating youth differently is intended to reduce reoffending and support 
positive development while still holding young people responsible for their actions. 
 
The primary criminal legislation that applies to youth in Canada is the Youth Criminal Justice 
Act (YCJA). The YCJA governs how individuals aged 12 to 17 are dealt with when charged 
with a criminal offence and sets out principles such as the use of extrajudicial measures, 
protection of privacy, reduced sentencing options, and alternatives to custody. While youth 
offences are based on the Criminal Code of Canada, the YCJA determines the procedures, rights, 
and sentencing principles that apply specifically to young persons. 
 
Courts recognize special considerations and alternatives to traditional sentencing in order to 
promote rehabilitation, accountability, and reintegration.  
• Special considerations include the offender’s age, level of maturity, mental health, 
cultural background, prior criminal record, and the circumstances surrounding the 
offence.  
• For youth, the law places emphasis on avoiding custody where possible and using 
responses that are proportionate to both the offence and the young person’s degree of 
responsibility.  
• Courts also consider the long-term impact of a criminal record and the offender’s 
potential for rehabilitation. 
 
Alternatives to sentencing may include extrajudicial measures, diversion programs, restorative 
justice approaches, community service, probation with treatment or counselling conditions, 
restitution to victims, and participation in education or skill-building programs. In Indigenous 
contexts, alternatives such as sentencing circles and community-based justice programs may be 
used. These approaches aim to address the underlying causes of offending behaviour, repair

3. Committee review 
4. Senate approval 
5. Royal Assent

Freedoms
